claims.text: Integrating experimental characterization with computational modeling can overcome the limited understanding of the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn HEA.
FeNiCrMn HEA eliminates the expensive Co element.
Eliminating Co from the alloy reduces costs.
The initial FeNiCrMn material is polycrystalline.
The initial FeNiCrMn material may be either a single-phase or multiphase solid solution.
A combined experimental and simulation approach is suitable for addressing the stated knowledge gap.
Controlling grain size can optimize the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn HEA.
Controlling phase composition can optimize the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn HEA.
Dislocation glide is a plausible deformation mechanism in polycrystalline FeNiCrMn HEA.
Grain-boundary sliding is a plausible deformation mechanism in polycrystalline FeNiCrMn HEA.
The approach will improve understanding of the yield strength and ductility of FeNiCrMn HEA.
The approach is predicted to increase yield strength by 10–20% relative to the baseline.
The approach is predicted to increase ductility by 5–10% relative to the baseline.
The experimental approach is limited to a maximum temperature of 1000 °C.
The experimental approach is limited to a minimum grain size of 10 μm.
The computational method is limited to a maximum strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The outcome predicts percentage increases in physical properties, but the baseline is defined as the current state of knowledge rather than as a material or processing condition with measurable yield strength and ductility.

The intervention is primarily a research methodology intended to improve understanding, yet the outcome and falsification rule treat applying that methodology as though it directly increases a sample's yield strength and ductility relative to a sample 'without' the methodology.
